authors: Elder, G. H.
title: The Life Course as Developmental Theory
design_or_method: Conceptual review of life course theory
key_finding: Lives are shaped by changing historical context; developmental concepts should apply across the life span; life course theory grew from following child cohorts into adulthood.

authors: Elder, G. H., Jr.
title: Time, Human Agency, and Social Change: Perspectives on the Life Course
key_finding: Not summarized (no abstract available); cited for life-course principles (timing, linked lives, agency) - recalled, verify against full text.
limitations: Crossref author metadata malformed (family name recorded as 'Jr.').
verification: crossref_verified 2026-11-12; note: Crossref author record malformed (given="Glen H. Elder", family="Jr."); normalized here.

authors: Rutter, M.
title: Transitions and Turning Points in Developmental Psychopathology: As applied to the Age Span between Childhood and Mid-adulthood
key_finding: Turning-point effects are a heterogeneous set of lasting changes; experiences linked to change usually involve particular qualities of experience affecting subsegments of the population rather than universal life-phase transitions; experiences may accentuate rather than alter characteristics.

authors: Laub, J. H.; Sampson, R. J.
title: TURNING POINTS IN THE LIFE COURSE: WHY CHANGE MATTERS TO THE STUDY OF CRIME*
design_or_method: Conceptual article with qualitative life-history data
key_finding: Distinguishes self-selection from cumulative processes; argues social capital and turning points explain change; incremental and abrupt change are structured by changes in adult social bonds.
limitations: Male, historical, delinquent sample; qualitative illustration.

authors: Sampson, R. J.; Laub, J. H.
title: A Life-Course View of the Development of Crime
journal: The ANNALS of the American Academy of Political and Social Science
key_finding: Proposes an age-graded theory of informal social control; revisits turning points from a time-varying view of life events; emphasizes human agency and random developmental noise.

authors: Clausen, J. S.
title: Adolescent Competence and the Shaping of the Life Course
key_finding: Not summarized (no abstract retrieved); cited for 'planful competence' in adolescence shaping later life course - recalled, verify against full text.

authors: Fuhrmann, D.; Knoll, L. J.; Blakemore, S.
title: Adolescence as a Sensitive Period of Brain Development
key_finding: Adolescence has been proposed as a second window of brain plasticity (memory, social stress, drug use) but concrete evidence for sensitive periods in adolescence is mostly lacking; experiments manipulating input across child/adolescent/adult groups are needed.

authors: Blakemore, S.; Mills, K. L.
title: Is Adolescence a Sensitive Period for Sociocultural Processing?
key_finding: The social brain undergoes structural and functional reorganization in the second decade, possibly reflecting a sensitive period for adapting to the social environment (framed as possibility).
limitations: Speculative about sensitive period; not about relationships with adults per se.

authors: Dahl, R. E.; Allen, N. B.; Wilbrecht, L.; Suleiman, A. B.
title: Importance of investing in adolescence from a developmental science perspective
key_finding: Argues adolescence is a maturational period in which lives can pivot rapidly and that there are windows of opportunity for policy affecting health, education and social/economic outcomes.
limitations: Advocacy review; windows asserted rather than tested.

authors: Knudsen, E. I.
title: Sensitive Periods in the Development of the Brain and Behavior
key_finding: Defines sensitive periods (experience has particularly strong effect during a limited period) and critical periods (experience essential and alters performance permanently); substantial plasticity remains after sensitive periods within constraints.
limitations: Definitions derived largely from sensory systems.

authors: Steinberg, L.
title: Cognitive and affective development in adolescence
key_finding: Describes adolescence as a critical or sensitive period for reorganization of regulatory systems, with both risks and opportunities, due to systems maturing on different timetables.

authors: Thomas, M. S. C.; Johnson, M. H.
title: New Advances in Understanding Sensitive Periods in Brain Development
key_finding: There are multiple varieties of and mechanisms for sensitive periods; many may be consequences of basic postnatal functional brain development processes.

authors: Frankenhuis, W. E.; Walasek, N.
title: Modeling the evolution of sensitive periods
key_finding: Reviews models of the environmental conditions under which sensitive periods evolve and how plasticity can respond optimally to experience.

authors: Gabard-Durnam, L.; McLaughlin, K. A.
title: Sensitive periods in human development: charting a course for the future
key_finding: Knowledge of human sensitive periods is limited in many domains and largely derived from animal methods; proposes approaches (deprivation/substitution paradigms, pharmacological manipulation, computational modeling) to study them in humans.

authors: Lerner, R. M.; Lerner, J. V.; Almerigi, J. B.; Theokas, C.; Phelps, E.; Gestsdottir, S.; Naudeau, S.; Jelicic, H.; Alberts, A.; Ma, L.; Smith, L. M.; Bobek, D. L.; Richman-Raphael, D.; Simpson, I.; Christiansen, E. D.; von Eye, A.
title: Positive Youth Development, Participation in Community Youth Development Programs, and Community Contributions of Fifth-Grade Adolescents: Findings From the First Wave Of the 4-H Study of Positive Youth Development
population: 4-H Study of PYD, 1,700 fifth graders and 1,117 parents
key_finding: Found five first-order factors (Five Cs) converging on a second-order PYD construct; PYD and youth development program participation independently related to youth contribution.

authors: Scales, P. C.; Benson, P. L.; Leffert, N.; Blyth, D. A.
title: Contribution of Developmental Assets to the Prediction of Thriving Among Adolescents
key_finding: Not summarized (no abstract retrieved); cited for developmental assets framework - verify against full text.

authors: Masten, A. S.
title: Ordinary magic: Resilience processes in development.
key_finding: Resilience is common and usually arises from normative human adaptational systems ('ordinary magic'); the greatest threats are those that compromise protective systems.

authors: Luthar, S. S.; Cicchetti, D.; Becker, B.
title: The Construct of Resilience: A Critical Evaluation and Guidelines for Future Work
key_finding: Addresses critiques of resilience (definitional ambiguity, heterogeneity, instability of the phenomenon) and proposes solutions; warns of conceptual and methodological pitfalls.

authors: Werner, E. E.
title: Risk, resilience, and recovery: Perspectives from the Kauai Longitudinal Study
key_finding: Several clusters of protective factors and processes enabled most high-risk individuals to become competent and caring adults.
limitations: Single cohort; specific protective factors not detailed in abstract.

authors: DuBois, D. L.; Holloway, B. E.; Valentine, J. C.; Cooper, H.
title: Effectiveness of Mentoring Programs for Youth: A Meta‐Analytic Review
key_finding: Modest or small benefit for the average youth; effects larger with more best practices and strong mentor-youth relationships; youth from environmental risk/disadvantage most likely to benefit; poorly implemented programs may harm youth with personal vulnerabilities.
limitations: Age moderation not reported in abstract.

authors: DuBois, D. L.; Portillo, N.; Rhodes, J. E.; Silverthorn, N.; Valentine, J. C.
title: How Effective Are Mentoring Programs for Youth? A Systematic Assessment of the Evidence
journal: Psychological Science in the Public Interest
key_finding: 73 evaluations (1999-2010). Modest average effect. Age coded in four groups (<8, 8-10, 11-14, 15-18): not among moderators associated with effect size; favorable effects within each age group; authors conclude benefits are not confined to a particular stage of development. Larger effects with higher-risk youth, more male youth, mentor advocacy/teaching roles, interest-based matching.
limitations: Only partial abstract available; no quantitative claims made here.
verification: crossref_verified 2026-11-12; full text read 2026-11-13 (copy supplied by the PI)

authors: Raposa, E. B.; Rhodes, J.; Stams, G. J. J. M.; Card, N.; Burton, S.; Schwartz, S.; Sykes, L. A. Y.; Kanchewa, S.; Kupersmidt, J.; Hussain, S.
title: The Effects of Youth Mentoring Programs: A Meta-analysis of Outcome Studies
key_finding: Statistically significant overall effect in the medium/moderate range relative to universal prevention benchmarks; larger effects for programs with more male youth, more male mentors or helping-profession mentors, and shorter meetings, and for questionnaire/self-report evaluations; authors urge realism about modest impact.
limitations: Abstract does not report age as a significant moderator; whether age was tested must be checked in full text.

authors: Grossman, J. B.; Tierney, J. P.
title: Does Mentoring Work?: An Impact Study of the Big Brothers Big Sisters Program
key_finding: Mentored youth were less likely to start using drugs/alcohol, hit someone, or skip school, more confident about school performance, and got along better with families.
limitations: Self-report outcomes; 18-month horizon; no attainment outcome.

authors: Herrera, C.; Grossman, J. B.; Kauh, T. J.; McMaken, J.
title: Mentoring in Schools: An Impact Study of Big Brothers Big Sisters School-Based Mentoring
key_finding: After year 1 mentored youth performed better academically, had better perceived academic ability and were more likely to report a 'special adult'; no improvements in effort, self-worth, relationships, or problem behavior; academic gains not sustained into year 2.

authors: Rhodes, J. E.; Spencer, R.; Keller, T. E.; Liang, B.; Noam, G.
title: A model for the influence of mentoring relationships on youth development
key_finding: Presents a conceptual model of the mentoring process and research on what makes mentoring relationships more effective.

authors: Grossman, J. B.; Rhodes, J. E.
title: The Test of Time: Predictors and Effects of Duration in Youth Mentoring Relationships
design_or_method: Secondary analysis of RCT by match duration
key_finding: Within the Big Brothers Big Sisters trial (N = 1,138, ages 10-16), benefits concentrated in matches lasting 12+ months; matches ending within 3 months were followed by declines in self-worth and perceived scholastic competence. Matches with 13-16 year olds were 65% more likely to end each period than with 10-12 year olds (2-year vs ~1.25-year expected length).
limitations: Duration not randomized (2SLS used to address selection); program sample
verification: crossref_verified 2026-11-12; full text read 2026-11-13 (copy supplied by the PI)

authors: Christensen, K. M.; Hagler, M. A.; Stams, G.; Raposa, E. B.; Burton, S.; Rhodes, J. E.
title: Non-Specific versus Targeted Approaches to Youth Mentoring: A Follow-up Meta-analysis
key_finding: Targeted, skills-based mentoring programs had an overall effect more than double that of non-specific relational programs, with moderator effects on academic, psychological and social functioning.
limitations: Program-level comparison, confounded with other program features.

authors: Schwartz, S. E. O.; Rhodes, J. E.; Spencer, R.; Grossman, J. B.
title: Youth Initiated Mentoring: Investigating a New Approach to Working with Vulnerable Adolescents
population: National Guard Youth ChalleNGe participants (N=1,173; qualitative n=30)
key_finding: More enduring youth-nominated mentoring relationships were associated with better retention of educational, vocational and behavioral outcomes at 3 years; relationships endured more when youth chose mentors themselves and with same-race mentors.

authors: van Dam, L.; Blom, D.; Kara, E.; Assink, M.; Stams, G.; Schwartz, S.; Rhodes, J.
title: Youth Initiated Mentoring: A Meta-analytic Study of a Hybrid Approach to Youth Mentoring
key_finding: Youth-initiated programs associated with positive outcomes, g = 0.30 overall and g = 0.40 controlling for possible selection bias; moderated by gender and year of publication.
limitations: Few studies; age moderation not reported in abstract.

authors: Heller, S. B.; Shah, A. K.; Guryan, J.; Ludwig, J.; Mullainathan, S.; Pollack, H. A.
title: Thinking, Fast and Slow? Some Field Experiments to Reduce Crime and Dropout in Chicago*
population: Economically disadvantaged male youth in Chicago (BAM) and detention center
key_finding: BAM reduced total arrests 28-35% and violent-crime arrests 45-50% during intervention, improved school engagement, and (study 1) increased graduation rates 12-19%; no positive evidence effects were due to a generic mentoring effect; suggestive support for slowing automatic thinking.
limitations: Mechanism evidence limited per authors; Chicago males only.

authors: Sinclair, M. F.; Christenson, S. L.; Evelo, D. L.; Hurley, C. M.
title: Dropout Prevention for Youth with Disabilities: Efficacy of a Sustained School Engagement Procedure
population: 94 students with learning and emotional/behavioral disabilities
design_or_method: Experimental, extended vs. ended intervention after grade 8
key_finding: Students continuing Check & Connect-type engagement intervention through grade 9 were more likely to be engaged in school on two of three measures; authors call for early and sustained support.
limitations: Small special-education sample; engagement not attainment.

authors: Rhodes, J. E.; DuBois, D. L.
title: Mentoring Relationships and Programs for Youth
key_finding: Associations between mentoring and outcomes are modest and depend on close, enduring connections; program effects small but increase with practices supporting relationship development.

authors: DuBois, D. L.; Silverthorn, N.
title: Natural Mentoring Relationships and Adolescent Health: Evidence From a National Study
design_or_method: Logistic regression with prior functioning controls
key_finding: Reporting a natural mentor was associated with favorable education/work outcomes (high school completion, college attendance), less problem behavior, better well-being and health; risk exposure effects were generally larger than mentoring's protective effects.

authors: Van Dam, L.; Smit, D.; Wildschut, B.; Branje, S. J. T.; Rhodes, J. E.; Assink, M.; Stams, G. J. J. M.
title: Does Natural Mentoring Matter? A Multilevel Meta‐analysis on the Association Between Natural Mentoring and Youth Outcomes
key_finding: Presence of a natural mentor associated with outcomes r = .106; relationship quality r = .208; largest effects for social-emotional and academic/vocational functioning; risk status did not moderate.
limitations: Mostly correlational primary studies; age moderation not reported in abstract.

authors: Erickson, L. D.; McDonald, S.; Elder, G. H.
title: Informal Mentors and Education: Complementary or Compensatory Resources?
key_finding: Mentors have a powerful net influence on educational success; youths with more resources are more likely to have mentors but those with fewer resources benefit more, particularly from teacher mentors (compensatory and complementary).

authors: Hurd, N.; Zimmerman, M.
title: Natural Mentors, Mental Health, and Risk Behaviors: A Longitudinal Analysis of African American Adolescents Transitioning into Adulthood
design_or_method: HLM growth curves over 5 years post-high school
key_finding: Having a natural mentor related to fewer depressive symptoms and less sexual risk behavior over time.

authors: Hurd, N. M.; Sánchez, B.; Zimmerman, M. A.; Caldwell, C. H.
title: Natural Mentors, Racial Identity, and Educational Attainment Among African American Adolescents: Exploring Pathways to Success
population: 541 academically at-risk African American adolescents (mean 17.8 at T1)
key_finding: Natural mentors were associated with higher long-term educational attainment via increased private regard and stronger beliefs in the importance of school.

authors: Timpe, Z. C.; Lunkenheimer, E.
title: The Long‐Term Economic Benefits of Natural Mentoring Relationships for Youth
design_or_method: Regression with moderation and NPV estimation
key_finding: Mentor presence alone did not significantly affect adult earnings; fatherless youth with a male mentor earned more, especially African American youth.
limitations: Observational; NPV estimates rest on strong assumptions.

authors: Fruiht, V. M.; Wray-Lake, L.
title: The Role of Mentor Type and Timing in Predicting Educational Attainment
design_or_method: Retrospective timing of when mentor became important (before/during/after high school)
key_finding: Teacher-mentors were more predictive of attainment than other mentor types; a mentor after high school predicted the most attainment; kin and community mentors appeared more important during and before high school respectively; consistent across ethnic groups.
limitations: Retrospective timing; selection and reverse causality (those continuing education meet post-HS mentors).

authors: Fruiht, V.; Chan, T.
title: Naturally Occurring Mentorship in a National Sample of First‐Generation College Goers: A Promising Portal for Academic and Developmental Success
key_finding: Adolescent mentorship moderated the association between parental college attendance and adult attainment; first-generation students received less identity-development support from mentors.

authors: Hagler, M. A.; Rhodes, J. E.
title: The Long‐Term Impact of Natural Mentoring Relationships: A Counterfactual Analysis
key_finding: Having a natural mentor in adolescence or emerging adulthood associated with higher attainment, volunteering, more close friends; weak-tie mentors (teachers, coaches, employers) associated with higher attainment and income, strong-tie mentors with more friends and lower income.
limitations: Counterfactual methods address only measured confounding.

authors: Miranda‐Chan, T.; Fruiht, V.; Dubon, V.; Wray‐Lake, L.
title: The Functions and Longitudinal Outcomes of Adolescents’ Naturally Occurring Mentorships
population: Nationally representative adolescents (Add Health per authors; verify)
key_finding: Having a community mentor in adolescence related to higher educational attainment, lower criminal activity, higher well-being, and romantic relationship satisfaction in adulthood; abstract opens by stating adolescence may be when nonfamilial adults are most influential (asserted, not tested).

authors: Raposa, E. B.; Erickson, L. D.; Hagler, M.; Rhodes, J. E.
title: How Economic Disadvantage Affects the Availability and Nature of Mentoring Relationships During the Transition to Adulthood
key_finding: Low-income adolescents had reduced access to natural mentors; their mentors were more often family/friends providing practical support and less often role models or career advisors.

authors: Bayer, A.; Grossman, J. B.; DuBois, D. L.
title: USING VOLUNTEER MENTORS TO IMPROVE THE ACADEMIC OUTCOMES OF UNDERSERVED STUDENTS: THE ROLE OF RELATIONSHIPS
design_or_method: Secondary analysis of RCT; 2SLS for relationship closeness
key_finding: Modest significant improvements in teacher-rated academic performance and scholastic efficacy; emotional closeness appears key, across relationship lengths.

authors: Roorda, D. L.; Koomen, H. M. Y.; Spilt, J. L.; Oort, F. J.
title: The Influence of Affective Teacher–Student Relationships on Students’ School Engagement and Achievement: A Meta-Analytic Approach
key_finding: Positive and negative teacher-student relationships associated with engagement (medium to large) and achievement (small to medium); stronger effects in higher grades overall, but negative relationships had stronger effects in primary than secondary school.

authors: Roorda, D. L.; Jak, S.; Zee, M.; Oort, F. J.; Koomen, H. M. Y.
title: Affective Teacher–Student Relationships and Students' Engagement and Achievement: A Meta-Analytic Update and Test of the Mediating Role of Engagement
key_finding: Not summarized (no abstract retrieved).

authors: Fredricks, J. A.; Blumenfeld, P. C.; Paris, A. H.
title: School Engagement: Potential of the Concept, State of the Evidence
key_finding: Engagement is presumed malleable and responsive to context; recommends multidimensional (behavioral, emotional, cognitive) study.

authors: Goodenow, C.
title: The psychological sense of school membership among adolescents: Scale development and educational correlates
key_finding: Not summarized (no abstract retrieved); cited for the PSSM school-membership scale.

authors: Allen, K.; Kern, M. L.; Vella-Brodrick, D.; Hattie, J.; Waters, L.
title: What Schools Need to Know About Fostering School Belonging: a Meta-analysis
key_finding: Not summarized (abstract elided by publisher in APIs consulted).

authors: Eccles, J. S.; Midgley, C.; Wigfield, A.; Buchanan, C. M.; Reuman, D.; Flanagan, C.; Mac Iver, D.
title: Development during adolescence: The impact of stage-environment fit on young adolescents' experiences in schools and in families.
key_finding: Some negative psychological changes in adolescence result from a mismatch between adolescents' needs and opportunities afforded by school and home environments (stage-environment fit).
limitations: Focus on middle-school transition, not grade 9.

authors: Neild, R. C.; Stoner-Eby, S.; Furstenberg, F.
title: Connecting Entrance and Departure: The Transition to Ninth Grade and High School Dropout
key_finding: Ninth-grade outcomes are not simply proxies for pre-high-school characteristics and add substantially to prediction of dropout; authors suggest focusing on the transition year.

authors: Benner, A. D.
title: The Transition to High School: Current Knowledge, Future Directions
design_or_method: Narrative review using life course theory
key_finding: Transitions can disrupt functioning across domains; the high school transition has received less attention than earlier transitions.

authors: Benner, A. D.; Graham, S.
title: The Transition to High School as a Developmental Process Among Multiethnic Urban Youth
key_finding: Adolescents doing well before the transition experienced disruptions in psychological functioning and grades at the high school transition, and many continued to struggle; especially challenging for African American and Latino students when same-ethnic representation declined.

authors: Wang, M.; Eccles, J. S.
title: Social Support Matters: Longitudinal Effects of Social Support on Three Dimensions of School Engagement From Middle to High School
key_finding: Multiple dimensions of engagement declined from 7th to 11th grade; teacher, peer and parent support predicted different engagement dimensions differently.

authors: Hamre, B. K.; Pianta, R. C.
title: Early Teacher–Child Relationships and the Trajectory of Children's School Outcomes through Eighth Grade
key_finding: Kindergarten teacher-rated relational negativity predicted academic and behavioral outcomes through grade 8, especially for children with high early behavior problems and boys, net of controls.

authors: Wentzel, K. R.
title: Social relationships and motivation in middle school: The role of parents, teachers, and peers.
key_finding: Not summarized (no abstract retrieved).

authors: Hill, N. E.; Tyson, D. F.
title: Parental involvement in middle school: A meta-analytic assessment of the strategies that promote achievement.
population: 50 studies of parental involvement in middle school
key_finding: Parental involvement positively associated with achievement except homework help; academic socialization had the strongest association and fits the developmental stage of early adolescence.

authors: Yeager, D. S.; Walton, G. M.
title: Social-Psychological Interventions in Education: They’re Not Magic
key_finding: Brief interventions targeting students' beliefs can yield lasting gains via recursive processes, but are context-dependent tools rather than quick fixes.

authors: Yeager, D. S.; Hanselman, P.; Walton, G. M.; Murray, J. S.; Crosnoe, R.; Muller, C.; Tipton, E.; Schneider, B.; Hulleman, C. S.; Hinojosa, C. P.; Paunesku, D.; Romero, C.; Flint, K.; Roberts, A.; Trott, J.; Iachan, R.; Buontempo, J.; Yang, S. M.; Carvalho, C. M.; ...; Dweck, C. S.
title: A national experiment reveals where a growth mindset improves achievement
population: Nationally representative sample of US 9th graders (per full text; verify)
key_finding: Under-one-hour online growth mindset intervention improved grades among lower-achieving students and increased advanced math enrollment; effects sustained where peer norms aligned with the message.

authors: Yeager, D. S.; Dahl, R. E.; Dweck, C. S.
title: Why Interventions to Influence Adolescent Behavior Often Fail but Could Succeed
key_finding: Proposes that traditional interventions work reasonably for children but less for middle adolescents, and that interventions aligned with adolescents' desire for status and respect may succeed.

authors: Bandura, A.
title: Self-efficacy: Toward a unifying theory of behavioral change.
key_finding: Not summarized (no abstract retrieved); cited for self-efficacy theory.

authors: Bandura, A.
title: Self-efficacy mechanism in human agency.
key_finding: Not summarized (no reliable abstract retrieved); cited for self-efficacy mechanism.

authors: Marcia, J. E.
title: Development and validation of ego-identity status.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
key_finding: Not summarized (no abstract retrieved); cited for identity status paradigm.

authors: Oyserman, D.; Bybee, D.; Terry, K.
title: Possible selves and academic outcomes: How and when possible selves impel action.
journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
key_finding: Linking academic possible selves to strategies increased academic initiative, test scores and grades, and reduced depression, absences and misbehavior; effects sustained over 2 years and mediated by change in possible selves.
limitations: Single trial; intervention delivered at a transition-adjacent grade.

authors: Mello, Z. R.
title: Gender variation in developmental trajectories of educational and occupational expectations and attainment from adolescence to adulthood.
key_finding: Adolescent educational and occupational expectations predicted corresponding adult attainment, with gender variation.

authors: Chetty, R.; Hendren, N.; Katz, L. F.
title: The Effects of Exposure to Better Neighborhoods on Children: New Evidence from the Moving to Opportunity Experiment
design_or_method: Randomized housing voucher experiment + tax data
key_finding: Moving to lower-poverty neighborhood before age 13 increased college attendance and earnings and reduced single parenthood; moving as an adolescent had slightly negative impacts; gains decline with age at move, implying exposure duration matters.

authors: Chetty, R.; Hendren, N.
title: The Impacts of Neighborhoods on Intergenerational Mobility I: Childhood Exposure Effects*
design_or_method: Movers design exploiting age at move; sibling comparisons
key_finding: (Abstract read from NBER working paper w23001 version.) Outcomes of children moving to better areas improve linearly with time spent there, approx. 4% per year of exposure; neighborhood effects operate mainly via childhood exposure.
limitations: Abstract read is from working-paper version; verify against QJE text.
verification: crossref_verified 2026-11-12; note: Abstract read from NBER Working Paper w23001 version.

authors: Cunha, F.; Heckman, J.
title: The Technology of Skill Formation
key_finding: Develops a stage-specific skill formation technology featuring self-productivity, dynamic complementarity and skill multipliers.
limitations: Model; abstract read via Semantic Scholar.

authors: Heckman, J. J.
title: Skill Formation and the Economics of Investing in Disadvantaged Children
population: Early childhood and adolescent intervention evidence
key_finding: Life cycle skill formation is dynamic; early inputs strongly affect the productivity of later inputs.
limitations: Short review; emphasis on early childhood.

authors: Cunha, F.; Heckman, J. J.; Schennach, S. M.
title: Estimating the Technology of Cognitive and Noncognitive Skill Formation
population: US child panel data (per full text; verify)
design_or_method: Structural estimation of multistage production functions
key_finding: Substitutability decreases in later stages for cognitive skills but increases in later stages for noncognitive skills; for some configurations it is optimal to invest relatively more in later childhood.
verification: crossref_verified 2026-11-12; note: Crossref record has no author list; authors taken from PubMed record PMID 20563300 (given names abbreviated there; full given names to verify).

authors: Chetty, R.; Jackson, M. O.; Kuchler, T.; Stroebel, J.; Hendren, N.; Fluegge, R. B.; Gong, S.; Gonzalez, F.; Grondin, A.; Jacob, M.; Johnston, D.; Koenen, M.; Laguna-Muggenburg, E.; Mudekereza, F.; Rutter, T.; Thor, N.; Townsend, W.; Zhang, R.; Bailey, M.; ...; Wernerfelt, N.
title: Social capital I: measurement and associations with economic mobility
population: 21 billion Facebook friendships, US ZIP codes
key_finding: Economic connectedness (share of high-SES friends among low-SES people) is among the strongest predictors of upward mobility; other social capital measures less so.

authors: McLanahan, S.; Tach, L.; Schneider, D.
title: The Causal Effects of Father Absence
key_finding: Studies using more rigorous designs still find negative effects of father absence, smaller than cross-sectional estimates; evidence strongest for high school graduation, social-emotional adjustment and adult mental health.
limitations: Design heterogeneity; timing of absence not summarized in abstract.

authors: Amato, P. R.
title: The Impact of Family Formation Change on the Cognitive, Social, and Emotional Well-Being of the Next Generation
key_finding: Examines how changes in family formation affect children's well-being and evaluates marriage-promotion programs (abstract is descriptive only).

authors: von Elm, E.; Altman, D. G.; Egger, M.; Pocock, S. J.; Gøtzsche, P. C.; Vandenbroucke, J. P.
title: The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement: guidelines for reporting observational studies
key_finding: STROBE: 22-item checklist for reporting cohort, case-control and cross-sectional studies.

authors: Robins, J. M.; Hernán, M. Á.; Brumback, B.
title: Marginal Structural Models and Causal Inference in Epidemiology
key_finding: Standard adjustment is biased with time-dependent confounders affected by prior treatment; marginal structural models estimated with IPTW address this.
limitations: Requires positivity and no unmeasured confounding.

authors: VanderWeele, T. J.; Ding, P.
title: Sensitivity Analysis in Observational Research: Introducing the E-Value
key_finding: Introduces the E-value: minimum strength of association an unmeasured confounder would need with exposure and outcome to explain away an association.
limitations: Does not address selection or measurement error.

authors: White, I. R.; Royston, P.; Wood, A. M.
title: Multiple imputation using chained equations: Issues and guidance for practice
key_finding: Guidance on MICE: imputation model specification, number of imputations, analysis and pitfalls.

authors: Rubin, D. B.
title: Multiple Imputation for Nonresponse in Surveys
journal: Wiley Series in Probability and Statistics
key_finding: Not summarized; foundational multiple-imputation text.

authors: Hamaker, E. L.; Kuiper, R. M.; Grasman, R. P. P. P.
title: A critique of the cross-lagged panel model.
key_finding: If constructs have trait-like stability, CLPM lagged parameters do not represent within-person effects; proposes random-intercept CLPM.

authors: Ben-Shlomo, Y.; Kuh, D.
title: A life course approach to chronic disease epidemiology: conceptual models, empirical challenges and interdisciplinary perspectives
key_finding: Not summarized (no abstract retrieved); cited for life-course conceptual models (critical period, accumulation, chains of risk) - recalled, verify against full text.
limitations: Crossref lists only Ben-Shlomo as author; Semantic Scholar lists Ben-Shlomo & Kuh.
verification: crossref_verified 2026-11-12; note: Crossref lists only Y. Ben-Shlomo; second author D. Kuh per Semantic Scholar record.

authors: Kuh, D.; Ben-Shlomo, Y.; Lynch, J.; Hallqvist, J.; Power, C.
title: Life course epidemiology: Figure 1
journal: Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health
key_finding: Glossary intended to advance dialogue on the life course perspective (defines critical/sensitive periods, accumulation per full text - verify).

authors: Mishra, G.; Nitsch, D.; Black, S.; De Stavola, B.; Kuh, D.; Hardy, R.
title: A structured approach to modelling the effects of binary exposure variables over the life course
population: MRC National Survey of Health and Development
key_finding: Recommends comparing nested models for accumulation, critical period and effect modification hypotheses against a saturated model; cumulative-score-only analyses can mislead.

authors: Smith, A. D. A. C.; Heron, J.; Mishra, G.; Gilthorpe, M. S.; Ben-Shlomo, Y.; Tilling, K.
title: Model Selection of the Effect of Binary Exposures over the Life Course
key_finding: LASSO approach identified the most suitable life-course hypothesis with high probability in moderate samples, less so for change hypotheses or highly correlated exposures.

authors: Smith, A. D. A. C.; Hardy, R.; Heron, J.; Joinson, C. J.; Lawlor, D. A.; Macdonald-Wallis, C.; Tilling, K.
title: A structured approach to hypotheses involving continuous exposures over the life course
population: Two empirical examples (incl. childhood family stress and adolescent depression)
design_or_method: Least angle regression extension to continuous exposures, confounding and missing data
key_finding: Extends structured approach; in example, a sensitive-period hypothesis (association strengthening with proximity of stressful events) best explained adolescent depression.
limitations: Model selection is not causal identification.

authors: Zhu, Y.; Simpkin, A. J.; Suderman, M. J.; Lussier, A. A.; Walton, E.; Dunn, E. C.; Smith, A. D. A. C.
title: A Structured Approach to Evaluating Life-Course Hypotheses: Moving Beyond Analyses of Exposed Versus Unexposed in the -Omics Context
population: Simulations (n=700) and ALSPAC-type empirical sample (n=703; verify cohort)
key_finding: Selective inference and max-|t| tests controlled familywise error with moderate power; SLCMA can examine time-dependent effects if applied appropriately.

authors: Smith, B. J.; Smith, A. D. A. C.; Dunn, E. C.
title: Statistical Modeling of Sensitive Period Effects Using the Structured Life Course Modeling Approach (SLCMA)
key_finding: SLCMA uses least angle regression and selective inference to compare life-course hypotheses (sensitive periods, accumulation) for repeated exposures; R code available.

authors: Hernán, M. A.; Robins, J. M.
title: Using Big Data to Emulate a Target Trial When a Randomized Trial Is Not Available: Table 1.
key_finding: Causal analyses of observational data should explicitly emulate a target trial, which structures comparisons of sustained treatment strategies and avoids common pitfalls.

authors: Rhodes, J.; Reddy, R.; Roffman, J.; Grossman, J. B.
title: Promoting Successful Youth Mentoring Relationships: A Preliminary Screening Questionnaire
population: Big Brothers Big Sisters youth in a national evaluation (N = 347; ages 9.4-15.9, mean 12.1)
key_finding: Youth age (median split) was unrelated to relationship quality; longer matches (13-19 months) reported higher quality on all four scales than 1-6 month matches.
limitations: Duration not randomized; youth in longer matches may differ; program sample
